claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel carries a native, thin Fe-oxide passivation layer formed during ambient exposure.
The native Fe-oxide layer on Q235 steel is sufficient to slow room-temperature corrosion.
The native Fe-oxide layer becomes unstable when Q235 steel is exposed to aggressive salts at 700–900 °C.
High-temperature salt exposure can produce phase transformations and selective dissolution in an alloy.
High-temperature chloride exposure causes phase transformation, dissolution, or spallation specifically of the Fe-oxide scale on Q235 steel.
Failure to form or retain a protective layered oxide microstructure accelerates degradation of Q235 steel.
Alloy chemistry can affect mass loss and corrosion performance in molten salts.
Materials with higher Cr content or stable multiphase oxide scales retain better corrosion protection than Q235 steel.
Annealed NiCoCrAlFe HEA coatings have a mixed BCC/FCC structure and better corrosion resistance than the comparison conditions reported in that coating study.
The proposed Q235 mechanism applies when molten salts or high salt vapor pressures are present at 700–900 °C.
The proposed mechanism should not apply when corrosive salt is absent or less aggressive.
The proposed mechanism should not apply to highly alloyed steels, HEAs, or specimens with artificially thickened or enhanced oxide scales.
Salt-exposed Q235 steel at 700–900 °C will exhibit greater mass loss than Q235 controls subjected to an identical thermal profile in an inert atmosphere.
Salt-exposed Q235 steel will show more fragmented or dissolved oxide scales and greater underlying metal degradation than the reference condition.
Unexposed or room-temperature Q235 steel will show minimal mass change and intact oxide coverage.
A controlled comparison should use Q235 specimens with native oxide intact, with salt-exposed and inert-atmosphere groups receiving the same thermal profile.
Mass change, SEM oxide morphology, and XRD phase analysis can jointly test the proposed scale-failure mechanism.
The mechanism would be falsified if salt-exposed Q235 retains scale integrity and has a mass-loss rate comparable to the inert-heated control.
